papers.why: The canonical AI formalization of shared plans, and a genuine alternative to joint-intention accounts. SharedPlans builds collaboration entirely out of individual attitudes — crucially Int.Th, intending that a proposition hold, which does not itself drive action but licenses meshing subplans, helping a partner, and keeping them informed. The authors are explicit that no unreduced notion of we-intention is required. The other half of the contribution is partiality: agents begin with incomplete recipes and no settled allocation of who does what, and elaborate the plan as they go. Long, and worth reading selectively, but the reductive-versus-primitive question it poses is still live in every model in threads B and D.

Evidence that commitment carries normative force, and a developmental constraint on what the construct has to be.

papers.why: The clearest existing instance of joint planning treated as a planning problem rather than a game-theoretic or attributional one. Dyads take turns building a road network to connect cities under a shared budget, over decision sequences up to length 16. The winning model, Collaborative Heuristic Tree Search, predicts the partner's next action using the same value function it uses for itself and evaluates its own moves by simulating the partner's response — joint planning as recursive tree search rather than as equilibrium selection. Fills the gap where hierarchical and resource-rational planning meets two agents.
